newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - Buba statement on Bonn gold plans.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Buba statement on Bonn gold plans.

text.p: The Bundesbank announced on Wednesday it rejected plans by the German government to revalue gold assets to help boost its finances in the run up to European Economic and Monetary Union.
Following is a list of analysts' reactions.
THOMAS MAYER, GOLDMAN SACHS IN FRANKFURT

"Following this advice the government will have a tough time to proceed with this plan. They will have to look for a face saving exit. I expect them to emphasise that they were going to achieve the 3.0 percent of GDP deficit (EMU target) all along."

"Bonn can still do it and the Bundesbank will do it. It sounds as though they are being dragged kicking and screaming but they will go ahead and do it. We've had a lot of the ramifications in the market already, spreads have narrowed to Bunds and Bunds are selling off. So you have to look at this as a weaker euro and broader EMU, and at some point they could bring Italy into this.

"We've already seen some fudges from France and Italy and the problem is that this is really a big fudge for the market. It undermines the credibility of the Bundesbank and German economic policy. It's almost EMU at any cost and it is a big cost."

"I think it would be very damaging for the Bundesbank and Bonn and Germany as a whole to force the Bundesbank to make these payouts. It's not in line with what the European Monetary Institute said. If they go ahead then it will increase money supply and there will be an impact on monetary supply numbers. There is a conflict. Without these payments it will become more difficult to fulfil the deficit criteria."

"Details aside, the most worrying aspect is the Bundesbank's assertion that Bonn's plan was an infringement of the Bundesbank's independence. That is why Bunds have sold off. It is now a case of open conflict between the two parties. In terms of EMU, the bottom line is that the government has made clear that EMU is going ahead, and the government can overrule the Bundesbank on this issue (of gold reserves). It makes little difference to the chances of Germany meeting the Maastricht criteria. It only affects the deficit indirectly and would not be enough to close the budget gap. The government has to find further ways of doing this, but it probably will succeed."
